baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Silencing the Past (1995) placed the archive inside the production of history: silences enter at 'the moment of fact creation (the making of sources)', 'fact assembly (the making of archives)', 'fact retrieval (the making of narratives)' and 'retrospective significance (the making of history in the final instance)'; 'in history, power begins at the source' and 'archives are the institutions that organise facts and sources' (all as quoted by Davidson, 2020); Stoler's 2002 essay cites it three times
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Davidson 2020 (read, unpaginated), which reproduces the four-moments passage as a block quotation ('Silences enter the process of historical production at four crucial moments: the moment of fact creation (the making of sources); the moment of fact assembly (the making of archives); the moment of fact retrieval (the making of narratives); and the moment of retrospective significance (the making of history in the final instance)') and quotes 'in history, power begins at the source' and 'archives are the institutions that organise facts and sources' as Trouillot's words; Beacon contents; Stoler 2002 nn. 24, 38, 49 (reference list read). Body unread; corrected after review (finding 13). Wording awaits re-verification on a library copy of Silencing the Past, ch. 1 (precedent: the Chandavarkar 1997 quotations in 1.152).
baseline_incident_edges.map_label: Silences and the making of archives, 1995

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: The Haitian Revolution as 'An Unthinkable History' (1995, ch. 3): the 'historical guild' facilitated 'the relegation to an historical backburner of the three themes to which [the Haitian Revolution] was linked: racism, slavery and colonialism' (p. 98, as quoted by Craipain); Ti dife boule (1977) told the revolution in Creole; Haiti: State against Nation (1990) its Duvalierist legacy
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Craipain 2024 (read in full), quoting p. 98 and dating Ti dife boule to the Brooklyn Koléksion Lakansièl, 1977; the Chicago obituary and finding aid for the 1977 and 1990 books; Bulamah, Goyatá and Pereira on the 1990 book as 'the classic' (para. 2, read). Chapter 3 unread.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: 'Anthropology and the Savage Slot: The Poetics and Politics of Otherness' (Global Transformations, 2003) and the book as a whole: 'Anthropology discovered globalization before the term became fashionable' (chapter abstract); the discipline's concepts of culture, modernity and globalization as 'North Atlantic universals' (as read by Bulamah, Goyatá and Pereira, 2020); 'Adieu, Culture: A New Duty Arises'
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Springer abstract of ch. 2 (read); Springer contents; Bulamah et al. 2020, para. 5 (read); Duke contents of Trouillot Remixed for the essay's place. The 'savage slot' thesis itself was not read; the label uses the title.
baseline_incident_edges.map_label: The savage slot and North Atlantic universals, 2003

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Global Transformations (2003): 'North Atlantic Fictions: Global Transformations, 1492–1945', 'A Fragmented Globality' and 'The Anthropology of the State in the Age of Globalization' set the North Atlantic's production of 'the West' against the anthropology of globalization (Springer description); Peasants and Capital (1988) placed Dominica 'in the World Economy'
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Springer book page (description and contents, read); the Chicago obituary for the 1988 book. Bodies unread.
baseline_incident_edges.map_label: The West as a North Atlantic fiction, 1988–2003

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Ti dife boule sou istwa Ayiti (Brooklyn, 1977), a Creole history of the revolution written in exile by a group that 'harbored an anti- or rather a counter-academism … to oppose the knowledge embargo imposed by the "official" venues of knowledge production' (Lyonel Trouillot, as quoted by Craipain); 'virtually absent from bibliographies in North Atlantic academia' until the 2021 translation
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Craipain 2024 (read in full), quoting the Liverpool edition's preface (p. xxiii) and Jonassaint's afterword (p. 182); the Chicago obituary; the finding aid ('fleeing the Duvalier regime', 1968).
baseline_incident_edges.map_label: A Creole history against the guild, 1977–2021

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Silencing the Past 'remains an unavoidable reference for anyone navigating the streams of Black and Caribbean studies in academia and beyond' (Craipain, 2024); Bulamah, Goyatá and Pereira read 'The Odd and the Ordinary' as challenging an exceptionalist image that isolates Haiti from its surrounding world (2020, paragraph 5)
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Craipain 2024 (read in full); Bulamah et al. 2020, paras 3–5 (read). Corrected after review (finding 7): the phrase 'dominated by Christianity, capitalism, and whiteness' (1990a: 7) describes the surrounding world, not Haiti's exceptionalist image, and is no longer quoted here.
baseline_incident_edges.map_label: Haiti in Black and Caribbean studies, 1990–2024

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: 'A critical indictment of Western historiography and its systematic disregard for Haiti's contribution to emancipatory struggles and decolonial politics', offering 'an eye-opening analysis of the epistemological failures and ideological maneuverings intrinsic to history telling as a professional activity' (Craipain, 2024); 'As Trouillot taught us, not all narratives or narrators are created equal'
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Craipain 2024 (read in full). Trouillot's own words for this claim are only Davidson's unpaginated quotations ('Power is constitutive of the story'). Wording awaits re-verification on a library copy of Silencing the Past, ch. 1 (precedent: the Chandavarkar 1997 quotations in 1.152).

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: 'The Presence in the Past' (1995, ch. 5), 'Good Day, Columbus: Silences, Power, and Public History (1492–1892)' and 'Abortive Rituals: Historical Apologies in the Global Era' (2000) took commemoration and apology as moments of 'retrospective significance (the making of history in the final instance)' (as quoted by Davidson, 2020); in Davidson's exposition, silences are produced and reproduced throughout any telling of a story
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Chapter and essay titles (Beacon and Duke contents, read); Davidson 2020 (read), whose block quotation gives the fourth moment in Trouillot's words; the sentence 'Silences are produced and reproduced throughout any telling of a story' is Davidson's own exposition, not a Trouillot quotation (corrected after review, finding 13). Thin: no body read. Wording awaits re-verification on a library copy of Silencing the Past, ch. 1 (precedent: the Chandavarkar 1997 quotations in 1.152).

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: O’Brien uses Trouillot’s account of unequal historical production and archival power to analyze local histories and public commemoration.
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Own selected public indexedxvii/xxiand56explicitly name Trouillot when widening historical production beyond professional historians, treating local histories as an archive, and considering public meanings made through commemoration. A particular theoretical resource, not sole genealogy or a claim that the full primary pages were read. Selected214indexednote names Silencing the Past,55; complete endnotes/edition and Trouillot original unread.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Schwartz and Cook put the archivist's own choices into 'the making of modern memory': archives 'are not passive storehouses of old stuff, but active sites where social power is negotiated', and appraisal, description and access shape collective memory (2002)
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Schwartz and Cook 2002 abstract (read); the memory entry's strand archive_authority (Combe, Derrida) is the existing hook. Trouillot's commemoration essays were removed after review (finding 9): p4A_rel_27 carries them.
relevant_group_routes.map_label: Archives in the making of memory, 2002

relevant_group_routes.relationship: The archive of Atlantic slavery as the field's hardest case: Hartman's 'Venus in Two Acts' (2008) and the 'critical fabulation' the MacArthur Foundation describes (2019); Fuentes's Dispossessed Lives (2016), which 'interrogates the archive and its historical production' for Bridgetown's enslaved and free women (publisher)
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: MacArthur's description of critical fabulation (read); Fuentes's publisher description (read). Hartman and Fuentes unread. Trouillot's clauses were removed after review (finding 9): p4A_rel_21 carries them.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Hartman's 'critical fabulation' and Fuentes's black-feminist reading of 'fragmentary sources' (2016) take the archive's violence as the problem of Black history
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: MacArthur's description (read); Fuentes's publisher description (read). The black entry's strand archives ('Collecting and diaspora bibliography') is the hook. Trouillot's clause was removed after review (finding 9): p4A_rel_25 carries it.
relevant_group_routes.map_label: The violence of the archive in Black history, 2008–16
